title.en: The Maihisikiri Takes the Woman for a Bush Spirit
title.zh: 邁希斯基里攜婦化為林鬼

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §§97-97A

summary.en: The Maihisikiri is a Yawahu wandering the bush that can assume the very face and body of a woman's husband; woe to the woman who yields to it, for she will die within days — unless she is shrewd enough to look at the left foot, which lacks its big toe. One woman was taken in three times; when at last she challenged it, the spirit confessed and led her away. Her husband found her lying in the distance laughing, all soft, without a single bone in her body — she had become a Bush Spirit herself, and told him, 'You will have to die before you can become one.'
summary.zh: 邁希斯基里乃林中鬼，能幻作婦人之夫；婦若信之，數日必死——惟察其左足無大趾者可辨。一婦三受其欺；末詰之，鬼自認而攜之去。夫尋至，見妻笑臥於野，遍體無骨——已化林鬼。婦曰：『夫須先死，方能為鬼。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Maihisikiri is a particular Yawahu wandering about the bush and in and among the trees, of which the native women have to be especially careful. Such spirits can assume the identical material appearance of their real husbands or lovers, but woe betide those poor women who yield to their solicitations, for they will surely die in a few days. The shrewd woman can always tell whether she is dealing with the real man or not — she has only to look at the left foot: in the case of a spirit wooer this is always minus the big toe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §97; not verbatim.

passages.text: A man went out hunting, leaving his wife behind; a Maihisikiri appeared, and believing it to be her husband, the woman allowed it to act like one. On the third visit, knowing her husband had gone to a distant locality, she asked: 'How can you be my husband? He is gone far away.' Only then did it admit it was a Bush Spirit in her husband's likeness, and told her to come away. When the real husband returned the house was empty; he found her prostrate, laughing because the Maihisikiri was sporting with her. When he seized her arm it was all soft, with no bones in it — she had not a single bone left in her body. 'I do not really want to leave you, husband, but the Maihisikiri is too strong for me. I am now a Bush Spirit. And though you must not be sorry for me, I am indeed sorry for you, for you will have to die before you can become one.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §97A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Always Hunted Scrub-Turkey

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §98

summary.en: A man celebrated for his skill in hunting maam (scrub-turkey) brought home four or five a day until people warned him he would get into trouble with the bird's 'mother' — the Spirit. He did not care. One evening, following the calling of the birds deeper and deeper into the forest, he found a woman's leg roosting among the branches: the arch Spirit of the maams. He shot the foot through the center; the leg fell and became an extraordinarily big scrub-turkey, which he cooked and ate whole, giving away not the smallest particle. Thereafter he hunted more successfully than ever, and feared nothing.
summary.zh: 一獵人善獵鷸，日獲四五隻；人誡其勿犯鳥之『母』——即鳥鬼——而彼不聽。一夜循鳴聲入深林，見枝上有婦人之足，乃鷸之大鬼。射其足心，足落地化為特大之鷸；烹而盡食之，分毫不與人。自後獵愈多，無所懼矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was a man celebrated for his skill in hunting 'maam' (scrub-turkey); he would regularly bring home four or five of these birds, and people warned him that if he continued in this way he would get into trouble with the maam's 'mother' — the Spirit — for killing so many of her brood. But he did not care, and went on destroying the birds in the same wasteful manner.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §98; not verbatim.

passages.text: One occasion he stayed out later than usual, tracking the calls deeper and deeper until he found himself deep in the forest. Locating the tree, he peered in among the branches to see where the bird was calling — but could see only a woman's leg. Recognizing this to be the arch Spirit of the maams, he took careful aim and shot an arrow right into the center of the foot. The leg fell down, and directly it touched ground changed into an extraordinarily big scrub-turkey, which he killed and carried home. His friends knew it at once to be the maam's 'mother', and advised him to cook and eat the whole of it himself, not giving away even the smallest particle. He did what was advised, and was ever after even more successful than before — and now that he had destroyed the maam-Spirit, he was not afraid of killing as many birds as he liked.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §98; not verbatim.

title.en: The Shrewd Little Boy and the Hebu

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §99

summary.en: Kau-nassa, a Hebu disguised as their old grandmother, led two little girls away 'to your mother' and drowned them in a closed basket dropped into a creek. At a second house the shrewd boy was told not to play behind her back — and so of course slipped behind, seeing the old woman's lower back aglow with the fire she carried there. Knowing her for a Hebu, he carried his little sister home, calling out her name: Kau-nassa! So angered and dismayed was the Spirit at being discovered that she burst into wind and flame and flew away.
summary.zh: 鬼卡烏納薩偽裝老嫗，誘二女往『見母』，織籃閉之沉於溪而溺之。至第二家，誡小兒毋戲其背——兒故潛至其後，見其下背火光熒然，知為林鬼。攜妹歸，呼其名曰：卡烏納薩！鬼羞怒，化風焰而飛去。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A woman having to go to make starch out of the ite tree left her little children, two girls, behind the house. While she was away Kau-nassa, a Bush Spirit, came along disguised as their old grandmother and said: 'Come along, my little girls. I will take you to your mother.' Instead she led them far into the bush to a creek, sat down and made a basket; when it was completed she told the youngsters to get inside, closed the top, and threw it into the water, where the children were soon drowned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §99; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kau-nassa then went to another house where a little boy and girl had been left in charge, similarly disguised as their grandmother. At the creek she said: 'You children must not play behind my back. Play in front of me where I can see you.' The very fact of being told not to go behind her made the boy all the more anxious to do what had been forbidden: he slipped away behind and saw the lower part of the old woman's back all aglow with the fire she carried there. He knew now that she was a Hebu, and getting back to his little sister, carried her home. But before going he called out, 'Kau-nassa! Kau-nassa!' So angered and dismayed was the Spirit at being discovered and hearing her name called that she burst into wind and flame and flew away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §99; not verbatim.

title.en: The Spirit's Brain and the Goat-Suckers

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克-加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §103

summary.en: Waiting for rain to draw land-crabs, a hunter pressed a calabash over his head; a Konoko-kuyuha marveling at his 'fine smooth head' was persuaded to have his own cut round and peppered, while the man slipped away. Years later the spirit recognized him by the pepper bushes grown on his skull and swore revenge. 'The person who really did it has been dead a long time,' said the man, leading him to a stack of deer bones; they danced with the bones rattling, and when the spirit bent his head low over the baking-stone the man crushed it. From each scattered piece of brain there grew a wokorai-yu, the goat-sucker — that is why we Indians dread these birds and leave them severely alone: they come from the spirits of the bush and give warning of evil.
summary.zh: 獵人候雨捕蟹，以瓢覆首；林鬼見其『光首』，羨而求己首亦環割敷椒；獵人遁去。多年後鬼認之，欲殺之。獵人曰：『其人久死矣』，引至鹿骨堆；共舞骨歌，鬼俯首近烤石，被擊碎腦——腦片各生一夜鷹。故印第安人畏夜鷹而不敢害之：彼等自林鬼而出，報凶之兆也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak/Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went out hunting for land crab, waiting for the rain to fall, for only under this condition does the animal creep out of its hole. When the rain fell it wet his hair; the huntsman, using his calabash like a cap, pressed it firmly down upon his head. A Konoko-kuyuha put in an appearance, and seeing the man in this guise could not help exclaiming: 'What a fine smooth head you have! How did you manage to get it?' The man told him he had just taken a knife and cut his head all the way round, and offered to do the same for the spirit, who was delighted, allowed the skin round his head to be cut and peppers rubbed over the raw surface to make it heal the quicker — groaning in pain while the huntsman quietly slipped out of sight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

passages.text: Many years later, the same man met the same Konoko-kuyuha and recognized him by the peppers on his head, which had grown into big bushes. 'You are the man who peeled off my head. I will kill you.' — 'No. The person who really did it has been dead a long time. Come with me and I will show you his bones.' He led him to a stack of deer bones; the spirit threw them one by one into his basket and said: 'Let us dance, and make his bones rattle.' Singing, 'It was you that peeled my head... How do you like to hear your own bones rattling for music?', they danced until the man directed the spirit onto a fine flat baking-stone and told him to bend his head lower, lower still — and suddenly crushed it thereon.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Spirit's brains were thus scattered, and from each piece there 'grew' a wokorai-yu — the goat-sucker. This is why we Indians always dread these birds, and leave them severely alone; they come from the Spirits of the Bush, and give us warning of evil — a token that we may expect trouble of various sorts.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §103; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mutilated Husband Is Made Whole

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §106

summary.en: A wife traveled in male attire to an all-male work camp, and when found out, the two men who coveted her tried three times to kill her husband — twice frustrated, the third time tied in a corial to drift out to sea, from which a tiger gnawed him free. A house-master who was really a Spirit sent him with a spirit friend to seek her; the guilty couple chopped him up with an ax, but the spirit restored him — again and again, until the keeper burned the body and scattered the ashes, and the spirit gathered the ashes in a palm leaf and made them into a living person again. Only spirits can do such things: the revived husband then destroyed his faithless wife and her paramour, whom their friends could not piece alive.
summary.zh: 婦扮男裝隨夫至男子聚作之所；事露，二男欲得其婦，三謀殺其夫——末縛之於舟，漂流出海，虎嚙繩縱之。一實為鬼之屋主遣鬼友偕往尋妻；奸夫婦以斧碎之，鬼復活之——三次皆然，末焚其屍而散其灰，鬼聚灰於棕葉，復成人形。惟鬼能為此。復活之夫乃誅其妻與其姦夫。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man told his wife he was going to another village to work for the headman; she was so importunate to come that he yielded and insisted on her traveling in male attire — hair cut short, breasts hidden with cotton and hog-tooth neck-chains, a strip of bark covering her nakedness. The others at the settlement wondered why the new-comer would never bathe with them, and set watch; discovering it was a woman, they determined on killing the husband so as to secure possession of the wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

passages.text: They tried twice, but each time something went wrong with their plans. The third time they tied him in a corial and let it drift out to sea, but the sea cast it back on shore, where a tiger, scenting him, gnawed through the ropes and set him free — for pure selfishness, telling his captive he now intended punishing him. 'Don't do that; haven't I been punished enough in losing my wife?' pleaded the man, and the tiger let him go. The house-master who received him was really a Spirit; he told the man to shut his eyes, and when he opened them again another Spirit was present to guide him to his wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

passages.text: The guilty couple, recognizing the husband, chopped him up with an ax — but the Spirit friend restored him to life. They killed him a second time; the Spirit again made him whole. A third time the keeper burned the body and scattered the ashes; this made no difference, for the Spirit collected the ashes together in a palm leaf and made them into a living person again. The resurrected husband, acting under advice, then destroyed his faithless wife as well as her paramour: their friends tried to piece the bits together and 'make them alive', but could not. It is only Spirits who can do such things.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §106; not verbatim.

title.en: How Pain, Misery, and Death Came into the World

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §108

summary.en: In the olden times there was no contention, all were happy, and no one became sick or died: the Yurokons came and lived among the Caribs as friends. One came as a woman with a baby at the breast; the pepper-pot burned her mouth, and while she went to the water for a drink some worthless woman threw her baby into the boiling cassiri pot. Stirring the pot, she found her child's body rise to the surface. Then she upbraided the people: 'Your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. You shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. And you men shall have great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' So fishing was made a toil of poisoning pools, and pain, misery, and death entered the world.
summary.zh: 上古無爭，人人安樂，無病無死：林鬼亦為友。一鬼幻為哺乳之婦；辣鍋灼口，取水間嬰兒被擲沸酒鍋中。攪酒而嬰屍浮。鬼怒咒曰：『汝等之子必死，令汝如我之泣；產子必受痛；捕魚必受勞。』於是毒魚為業，苦難與死亡遂入世。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically. Origin-of-death cluster parallel.

passages.text: In the olden times, there was no contention, all were happy, and no one became sick or died. It was then that the Yurokons used to come and live among us as our friends and associates; they were short people like ourselves. One Yurokon in particular used to come and drink paiwarri with my people regularly once a month. The last time he came, he appeared as a woman with a baby at the breast.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Caribs gave her of the pepper-pot, into which she dipped the cassava; it was so hot that it burned the inside of her mouth and 'heart', and this made her ask for water. Leaving her baby up at the house, she went down to the waterside and quenched her thirst. On her return her little child was nowhere to be seen, because during her absence some worthless woman among the company had thrown it into the boiling cassiri pot. By and by Yurokon went to stir the cassiri with the usual paddle-spoon, and, while she stirred, the body of her baby rose to the surface.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

passages.text: She wept, and then, turning on the people, upbraided them: 'Why have you punished me in this way? I have never had a bad mind against any of you, but now I will make you pay me. In future your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. And when children are born to you, you shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. Furthermore, I will give you great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' — for in those days the Caribs only had to bail the water out of the streams and pick up the fish left exposed at the bottom, putting the water back to breed fish once more. Yurokon altered all this, made fish-poisoning the toil it now is, killed the worthless Indian who had thrown her boy into the cassiri — and pain, misery, and death entered the world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §108; not verbatim.

narrative.en: The Caribs of the Pomeroon district tell that in the olden times there was no contention: all were happy, and no one became sick or died. In those days the Yurokons — the hairy little forest spirits, short people like the Caribs themselves — used to come and live among men as friends and associates. One Yurokon in particular came regularly once a month to drink paiwarri with the narrator's people. The last time he came he appeared as a woman with a baby at the breast. The Caribs gave her pepper-pot, into which she dipped her cassava; it burned her mouth and 'heart', and she asked for water, was told there was none, and went down to the water-side with her calabash, leaving the baby at the house. While she was gone some worthless woman among the company threw the child into the boiling cassiri pot. When she returned and stirred the drink with the paddle-spoon, the body of her baby rose to the surface. She wept, then turned on the people with the curse that re-ordered the world: 'Why have you punished me in this way? I have never had a bad mind against any of you, but now I will make you pay me. In future your children shall all die, and this will make you weep as I am weeping. And when children are born to you, you shall suffer pain and trouble at their birth. Furthermore, with regard to you men, I will give you great trouble when you go out to catch fish.' So fishing, which in those days meant simply bailing out a stream and picking the fish from the exposed bed before letting the water back to breed again, became the toil of poisoning pools with roots; and sickness, the pain of childbirth, and death entered the world — a Guianese parallel to the world-wide origin-of-death tales in which a spirit's child is killed and the loss is repaid in the only coin mortals have.

functions: Origin-of-death tale: explains mortality, the pain of childbirth, and the labour of fish-poisoning as a single compensation for the murdered spirit-child
Codes hospitality: guests — even disguised spirits — must not be wronged, for the wronged spirit's curse binds the whole community
Sanctions food-processing taboos around menstruation, pregnancy, and drinking-feasts within which such 'worthless women' offences were policed
Anchors the ritual authority of the piai, whose spirit-friends are the Yurokons now estranged from men

variants.name: Kururumanni version (Arawak, after Schomburgk)
variants.text_tradition: Arawak, recorded by Schomburgk and summarised by Roth
variants.summary: Kururumanni came to earth to see what the Arawaks were doing, found them so bad that he wished to destroy them, and took away their everlasting life, bestowing it on the creatures that cast their skins — snakes, lizards, and cockroaches.

variants.name: Tamanac version (after Humboldt)
variants.text_tradition: Tamanac, recorded by Humboldt, summarised in Roth 1915
variants.summary: Amalivaca, departing across the salt water, sang to the Tamanacs 'You will change your skins' — perpetual youth — until one doubting old woman cried out, and he revoked the blessing: 'You shall die!'

variants.name: Warrau version (after Roth)
variants.summary: A man who married a Water Spirit disobeyed her one command — that at her moon-sickness she must stay in the hut — and she died in the women's out-house; her father decreed that sickness, accident and death should henceforth come to the Warraus from the Water People.

title.en: Why the Drink Turned Sour

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §109

summary.en: When anything went wrong with the fermentation of their drinks, the Indians ascribed it to spirit machinations. A traveler sleeping on the manicole rafters of a neighbor's house watched a band of Hebus arrive, bathe, and carouse over the big jar of drink prepared for the morrow's festivities, a little labba playing for their dance with its own grunting tune. At daybreak the spirits left, and the household, returning, found the watcher's warning waiting for them: the liquor was thrown away, for the widow of the house had received a token from her dead husband that the Hebus would spoil the drink.
summary.zh: 酒之變酸，皆歸鬼祟。一客夜宿鄰家椽上，見群鬼至，浴而共飲明日祭宴之酒，以豬蹄獸之呼聲為舞樂。黎明鬼散；家主歸，客誡之，遂傾酒——蓋家中寡婦已得其亡夫之兆：『鬼將敗我酒。』

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went one day to visit some neighbors and, finding them all out, made arrangements to sleep there. He drew himself up on the manicole rafters and turned in. In this house there was a big jar in which drink was being prepared in anticipation of next day's festivities. He had not been long on the manicole flooring before he saw a lot of Hebus enter the place: 'Hullo! here is some drink. Let us bathe first, and then come and taste it. It were a pity to let it spoil.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §109; not verbatim.

passages.text: They all washed their skins and returned for a good carousal; feeling the want of music they arranged with a labba to play for them — all the tune it could play was its usual grunt, but they enjoyed their dance. Our friend watched them until daybreak, when they departed, the little labba sneaking away behind a plantain tree. Later the household returned, saying just as the Spirits did: 'Let us bathe first and then drink. It were a pity to let it spoil.' But the watcher warned them not to touch the liquor, for he had seen the Hebus sipping it. They therefore threw all the drink away — for a widow among them had received a sign: as she wept for her late husband he suddenly appeared and told her to cease to cry, 'Yes, I knew the Hebus were going to spoil our drink.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §109; not verbatim.

title.en: The Yawahu-Arrow: Why Children Become Sick and Cry

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §110

summary.en: An Indian built a scaffold on a locust tree to shoot small deer and, waiting bow in hand, saw a Yurokon woman come with a baby slung over her breasts to gather the fallen locust seed. As she gathered, the Indian shot the child. She could find no arrow on it, but the piai of her tribe sucked the invisible weapon out of the child's flesh. 'Very well,' exclaimed the mother; 'just as that Indian shot my boy, so will my husband shoot his people's children, and make them cry without anyone knowing the reason.' So the Yawahu-shimara, the Spirit's Arrow, entered the world.
summary.zh: 一獵者登洋槐樹臺射鹿；林鬼婦攜嬰拾落子。獵者射其嬰。母遍尋無箭，族中醫師乃吸出隱形之箭以示之。母曰：『恰如此人射我兒，我夫亦將射其族之小兒，令其無故而啼。』自是鬼箭入世。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: An Indian went into the forest to hunt small deer, and for this purpose built a scaffold upon the trunk of a locust tree. Sitting on top of it, bow and arrow in hand, he waited for the animals to come and eat the seeds that had fallen around. By and by a Yurokon woman came along with a baby slung over her breasts and a quake over her forehead; she was fond of locust seed, and put her baby down on the ground right below the spot where the Indian was seated, then went round the tree picking up the seeds and gathering them into her basket.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §110; not verbatim.

passages.text: While she was thus engaged the Indian shot the child, making it cry. The mother rushed back to find her infant screaming for no apparent cause; she felt it all over but could discover no arrow. So she took it to the piai of her tribe, who soon discovered what was the matter and sucked the weapon out of the child. 'Very well,' exclaimed the mother; 'just as that Indian shot my boy, so will my husband shoot his people's children, and make them cry without anyone knowing the reason.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §110; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Killed by Her Husband's Spirit

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §113

summary.en: A party of Arawak men were murdered at Morawinni; all their Pomeroon wives took other men except one faithful one. At night she heard the harri-harri flute playing on the river, coming nearer — her husband's spirit, come back sick, telling how the party had all been killed. He asked her to pick off the 'dog-fleas' biting his back; by firelight she saw them: worms, crawling in and out of a dead man's body. She spat quietly into a pool till the spittle could answer 'No, No! there are no dog-fleas there' in her stead, and fled. 'I am dead. But though dead, I am looking for her, and I shall soon make her dead also.' Hiding in an old armadillo hole, she escaped him that night — but she soon became sick, and died.
summary.zh: 眾夫被害於摩拉溫尼；眾妻皆再嫁，惟一婦守節。夜聞河上笛聲近——乃夫之魂，述眾人皆亡。魂索妻拾其背『犬蚤』；燭照之，見為蛆蟲出入。婦唾涎為池，代己應答，潛逃入犰狳穴。魂曰：『吾死矣，然必索其命。』婦是夜得脫，未幾病而卒。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A party of Arawaks, all of them married men, once went to Morawinni, on the way to the Berbice, where they were murdered. Their wives whom they had left behind took other men, all except one, who was very sorry at losing her husband and would not take another. When night came on, she heard the harri-harri flute playing in the river, the sound gradually coming nearer. Recognizing it as her husband's, she said to her child: 'That tune is like what your father used to play. Perhaps he alone was saved.' As a matter of fact it was indeed the man's Spirit trying to come back home again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113; not verbatim.

passages.text: He tied up his corial, came up to the house, and told her to sling his hammock, for he was come back sick, and related how he and his party had all been killed. 'Go and fetch a light: there must be a lot of dog-fleas about; they are biting my back terribly.' But instead of dog-fleas it was worms that were gnawing into him; by the fire-stick his wife could see them crawling in and out. Now she knew that it was her husband's Spirit, not his Body, that had returned, and a token of something that was to happen.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113; not verbatim.

passages.text: She began to spit quietly in one spot until there was quite a pool of spittle, slipped away, and hid in an old armadillo hole while the spirit passed on. When it again asked her to pick off the dog-fleas, it was the Spittle that answered 'No, No! There are no dog-fleas there' — until it was dried up and could speak no more. Then the Spirit followed her tracks in the darkness, and she heard him say to himself: 'I am dead. But though dead, I am looking for her, and I shall soon make her dead also.' She escaped him that night and reached the next settlement — but the Spirit had said what was true: she soon became sick, and died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wages of Stealing: Eighteen Men, One Pond of Pirai
title.zh: 竊食之報：十八盲者與食人魚之池

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §113A

summary.en: Twenty hunters found victuals stacked on their trail — drink, meat, everything an Indian can desire. Eighteen ate of what did not belong to them; two refused and camped apart. In the night the Hebu came with a light and, extinguishing it, sucked out each sleeper's eyes like the flesh of a crab-claw. The blinded eighteen were led home on a string made of bow-strings — but the two sound men led them instead to a pond of pirai fish, threw timber splashes over their heads, and let the blind ones rush in and be destroyed, punished for taking food which was not theirs.
summary.zh: 二十獵者途遇陳食；十八人食之，二人不食而別營。夜間鬼執燭至，逐一吸去十八人之目，如吮蟹肉。盲者以弓弦相牽，令二人引歸——二人竟引至食人魚之池，擲木使響，盲者盡赴池中為魚所噬，此其竊食之報。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Twenty men started out to hunt bush-hog, taking their hammocks, and camped on the tracks at nightfall. Next morning about mid-day they noticed plenty of victuals stacked ready for consumption: drink and meat, plenty of everything that an Indian can desire. Some said 'Of course I am going to eat. Isn't it all ready prepared for us?' Others said: 'No. It is not ours. We will not eat what does not belong to us.' The wishes of the majority prevailed, and all except two partook of the fine food.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113A; not verbatim.

passages.text: The two who had declined to eat erected their benab apart; during the night the Hebu came along with a light in his hand, approached the eighteen sleeping men, extinguished the light, and — sucking the air through his half-closed hand — extracted each victim's eyes, just as we suck the flesh out of one end of a crab-claw. Next morning each of the eighteen woke exclaiming 'Me, eye out!' So as to get home, the blind ones had bow-strings tied end to end into one long string, holding on while the two sound men led the way.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113A; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the two led them, not homeward, but to a big pond containing a large number of pirai fish. Telling the blind ones they were about to cross a river and must rush in straight ahead when they heard a splash, the two stepped behind and threw heavy pieces of timber over their heads. As these fell into the water there was of course a splash, and all the eighteen rushed ahead only to knock up against one another in the middle of the pond, where the voracious fish mutilated and destroyed them. They were thus punished for taking food which did not belong to them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Singing Brother Changed into a Beast

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §113B

summary.en: Two brothers went in their corial to shoot morokot fish; the younger steering began to sing, and would not heed his brother's warning that the noise would spoil the fishing. Left on the bank, he raised his singing higher and higher — a rolling, roaring noise that frightened even the father who went to see. The Hebu had changed him into an evil beast, ready to kill anybody and anything; he was already beast from the neck downward, with two big teeth on his belly. Waiting in the clearing, the father and the elder brother shot him — lucky they did, or he would have killed them. Had he kept quiet when his brother warned him, all this trouble would not have happened.
summary.zh: 二兄弟乘舟射魚；弟掌舵而歌，不聽兄誡。留於岸上，其歌愈高，吼聲震野，父往視亦懼。林鬼已化之為惡獸，頸以下皆獸形，腹有二巨牙。父與兄候於空地而射殺之——非此則二人皆死。若弟初聽兄言，何至於此。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Two brothers set out in their corial to shoot morokot fish, after telling their old father where they were going. The younger, who was steering, started singing. 'Don't do that,' said his brother; 'if you make that noise, we shall get no fish and father will be disappointed.' But he would not heed, and the elder one said: 'This won't do. I will leave you on shore.' With an 'All right; leave me here' the younger stayed on the bank, raising his singing to an even higher pitch.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113B; not verbatim.

passages.text: The elder brother recognized that this was a token of something about to happen, paddled on alone, shot three morokot now that there was no noise, and returned to pick up his brother — only to find him singing more high than ever, such a rolling and a roaring that he became frightened and went home without him. The old father would not believe it and went to see for himself, following the crushed tracks of a big carcass. 'Come! Come!' — but all the reply was a terrible roar. The son had been changed by the Hebu into an evil beast, ready to kill anybody and anything.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113B; not verbatim.

passages.text: On reaching the waterside again the father told his elder boy to be prepared to shoot as soon as the creature put in an appearance. At last it came out into the clearing and they shot him. It was lucky they did so, because he was already changed into a beast from the neck downward, with two big teeth on his belly. Had he kept quiet when his brother warned him, all this trouble would not have happened.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §113B; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Dined After Dark

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §114

summary.en: In the olden times it was strictly taboo for anyone to take a meal after nightfall; the punishment for infringement was transformation into some bird or beast. Two friends fishing by night found a bunch of ripe kokerite nuts; warned that the sun was sinking, one would not stop — the nuts were so sweet — and kept chewing long after dark. His friend heard him breaking them in his teeth, not with a stone, and lit his wax torch: instead of a man, a tiger crunching the seeds. The mother, refusing to believe, went alone toward the deep rough voice and the tiger sprang upon and killed her. She was punished because she would not trust the man who told her the tiger really was her son.
summary.zh: 古俗夜後不得進食；犯者化為鳥獸。二漁友夜得柯基里棕之堅果；日沉而不止，其味甘也。友聞其以齒碎果，燃蠟炬照之——非人乃虎。母不信，循聲獨往，虎躍而殺之。蓋母不信其子已為虎，故受其報。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In the olden times it was strictly 'taboo' for anyone to take a meal after nightfall, the certain punishment for infringement being the transformation of the offender into some bird or beast. There were once two fishers, friends. They went out to a neighboring creek, built a shed, and set their hooks, remaining there all night. Resting at the benab they noticed near by a kokerite palm with a splendid bunch of ripe nuts; these they cut down and began eating after breaking them on the stones. They were delicious, and they continued eating until one noticed the sun was about to sink on the horizon and warned his friend to stop, advising him to turn into his hammock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §114; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the warning was unheeded: he said they were so sweet that he couldn't stop, and he continued breaking and chewing the nuts until long after dark. Then, all of a sudden, instead of breaking the nuts with a stone, his friend in the hammock heard him breaking them in his teeth; knowing well that no Indian could do this, he lit his wax torch, and instead of a man saw a tiger crunching the seeds. He slipped out, wandered about till dawn, picked up his hooks, and hurried home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §114; not verbatim.

passages.text: When his mate's mother asked why her son had not accompanied him, he told her he had persisted in eating after dark and was now a Yawahu tiger. She would not believe him, though a deep rough voice answered her hail with 'That's your son.' Wanting to see for herself she went alone into the bush in the direction of the sound, strongly warned not to — and at last met the tiger, who sprang upon and killed her. The mother was punished because she would not trust the man when he told her that the tiger really was her son.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §114; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Haimara Came to Have Such Fine Big Eyes

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §115

summary.en: A hunter met a hairy Konoko-kuyuha making a basket — an eye-socket basket — and warned his family not to sleep that night. They laughed, slept, and had both eyes stealthily removed from every hammock, placed in the completed basket. The warned man tied them one to another to a tree by the water, but all slid under and changed into fish — the one exception, tied to the tree, turned only halfway. In time the Spirit took pity on the last man, completed his transformation, and gave him back his own two eyes, 'all very fine and large' — the eyes of the haimara fish. And their old friend, returning at last, cut the rope and let the fish play about in the water. They were punished for their unbelief.
summary.zh: 獵者遇毛鬼織『眼窩籃』，誡家人夜勿睡；眾笑而睡，目盡被竊入籃。獵者以繩相繫於水邊樹；眾入水化魚，惟繫樹者半化。鬼憫之，完其化而還其二目——特大而美，即海瑪拉魚之目。獵者斷繩縱魚游於水。眾之不信，其罰也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Returning home from the bush one afternoon, a hunter met a Konoko-kuyuha making a basket — a spirit with the entire face, body, and limbs covered with thick hair. He asked what it was doing, but the only word it deigned to answer was bako, the Arawak term for an eye-socket, applied to a basket with an oblong concavity in its base. He advised his family strongly not to go to sleep that night, because it, whatever it was, might pay them a surprise visit; but they all laughed at him and soon fell asleep, while he clambered up into the roof.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §115; not verbatim.

passages.text: The spirit entered the house, stealthily approached each hammock, and removed both eyes of the snoring occupant without waking him, placing them carefully in the now completed basket. Next morning all the people awoke to find they could see nothing. 'We are not fit to live on the land; take us to some waterside.' He tied them one to the other, and the last one to a tree; but they had all in the meanwhile been under water and changed into fish, the one exception, able to get in only up to his middle, turning but halfway into a fish.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §115; not verbatim.

passages.text: He was a long time returning — so long that the Spirit took pity on the last man, completed his transformation, and gave him back his own two eyes, which are all very fine and large, especially for a haimara fish. And when their old friend did return at last, he cut the rope from the tree, allowing the haimara and other fish to play about with perfect freedom in the water, where they have since remained. They were punished for their unbelief.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §115; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wrong Rattle, the Bush-Hog, and the Baby

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §116

summary.en: Siwara, a Hebu, came as a courteous 'cousin' to two girls minding the house, left a powis, and later — offered the elder daughter by a muddled father — became a son-in-law who hunted so well his game bags never failed. He taught the brothers-in-law to shoot bush-hog with paired rattles: one to call the timid kind, one to call the savage, one of each to drive away. Warned never to touch them, a brother-in-law shook the wrong maraka while Siwara was away: the savage bush-hogs came trooping in from near and far, and the mother, forgetting her baby in the scramble up the trees, lost it — the hogs tore it in pieces and devoured it. Siwara drove the brutes off with the proper rattle, blamed them for disobeying his orders, and left them forever. It is very hard for them to get food now.
summary.zh: 鬼西瓦拉扮『表兄』訪二女，後聘其姊為妻，善獵無虛日。教內兄弟以雙鈴獵野豬：一呼馴者，一呼猛者，各有驅散之鈴。誡勿妄搖；然內兄於其外出時誤搖猛豬之鈴，猛豬四面而至，家人攀樹而逃，母忘其嬰，嬰為豬所裂而食。西瓦拉以正鈴驅之，怒其違命而去。自是彼等謀食甚艱。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man with his wife and two sons went to a neighboring settlement to join a drink-party, leaving their two girls busy making cassiri. Going to fetch water they heard a peculiar cry — really Siwara, the Hebu, misleading them by imitating the call of the oto bird; they challenged it in the usual way, shouting 'Don't cry, but show yourself, or kill something for us.' The stranger appeared at the house as a courteous young 'cousin', was offered cassava and drink, and next morning warned the girls not to tell their parents of his visit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §116; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the parents returned they found a dried powis, and the girls lied that they had taken it from an oto hawk — until the old father, chewing his portion, came across a piece of kokerite arrow in it. 'If an oto killed the bird, how did this kokerite arrow get in?' He made them call the visitor in, and, still muddled from the drinking party, offered his elder daughter to Siwara, who liked her very much. Thus the Hebu obtained his wife — and proved a very good husband and son-in-law, always returning from his hunting expeditions well loaded with game. He also took the trouble to teach his wife's brothers how to shoot bush-hog, shaking his maraka (rattle) so that the beasts came rushing up in obedience to the summons.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §116; not verbatim.

passages.text: Among his property he hung up four rattles for bush-hog — one rattle to call the timid kind, one to call the very savage, and one of each kind to drive the beasts away — warning his wife's people that on no account must they touch these marakas during his absence. While he was away cutting a field a brother-in-law could not resist scrutinizing one, and started shaking it: it was the wrong rattle, the one for the wild bush-hog, and these savage beasts came trooping in from near and far, leaving the household barely time to escape up the nearest trees. In the hurry the mother forgot her baby, which the hogs tore in pieces and devoured. Siwara came, shook the proper rattle, drove the brutes away, blamed them for disobeying his orders, and left them — it is very hard for them to get food now.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §116; not verbatim.

title.en: The Killing of the Bush Spirit and His Wife

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §117

summary.en: A hunter's wife was left at the benab with no warning; a Konoko-kuyuha visited, said it would return in the evening, and — the husband snoring too soundly to wake — broke his neck, drank his blood, and left him dead, seeking the wife in vain. Next day her brother went with her to the same benab, had her tell the spirit that her husband was alive and glad to see him in the evening, made a special arrow, and taught her to lead the spirit in a dance. Circling closer and closer to the ambush, she held his hands as instructed; the arrow flew through the wicked spirit, and when it protested 'I did nothing to you', she answered 'No, indeed, but you wanted to.' The spirit's moaning wife came for blood payment, and the brother shot her too.
summary.zh: 獵者之妻無誡而留守；林鬼夜至，夫酣睡不能醒，鬼折其頸飲其血而殺之，尋妻不獲。翌日兄偕妹返故棚，令鬼信其夫尚存，晚當見之；兄製特箭，教妹與鬼共舞。妹引鬼近伏處，箭發貫之。鬼曰：『吾未嘗害汝，何欲殺我？』妹曰：『然汝欲害我。』鬼妻來索命債，兄亦射殺之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went out hunting one day and took his wife with him, leaving her as usual one morning at the benab. A Kokono-kuyuha came to the house and asked how she fared and where her man had gone; it went away mentioning that she might see him again in the evening — greedy, and thinking it less trouble to kill and eat them both at one and the same time. When the husband did return he would not believe her warning, and fell asleep snoring heavily.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117; not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the Konoko-kuyuha came along, giving warning of his approach by striking the buttresses of the trees. The wife tried to wake her husband, but he slept too soundly; she quickly hid herself. The Bush Spirit approached the sleeping man's hammock, failed to wake him, broke his neck, drank his blood, and left him dead — then wandered all over the place looking for the wife, saying: 'If I had known that she intended giving me the slip, I would have finished her off this morning.' She remained hidden until dawn, buried the body, and ran home to her brother, who was exceedingly angry and determined upon killing the Spirit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he went with his sister to the same benab and left her by herself there, instructed to fool the spirit by saying her husband was alive and would be glad to see him in the evening. He made a special arrow and showed her how to tempt the Spirit into a dance, holding his hands without embracing him too closely so the arrow might not strike her. Darkness fell; she obtruded all her charms and the spirit only too readily agreed, circling round and round, closer and closer to where the brother lay ambushed. The special arrow flew right through the wicked Spirit. 'I did nothing to you, to make you wish to kill me,' he reproached her. 'No, indeed, but you wanted to.' His wife soon came along crying that she must get payment for her husband — and the brother shot her also.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Kills the Hebu

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §117A

summary.en: Going to a party, a man left his wife to follow in the afternoon; another man came and threatened to kill her unless she came to his place. He was really a Hebu. At his house, with its dried game, fish, birds, and human flesh, she planned her revenge: when he called her into his hammock she refused to lie down because he was covered over so much with hair, asked where to find a bamboo-knife, and shaved his face — holding up his chin, she stuck the knife into his throat and killed him, then fled with her child to her husband at the drink-party. When the sport was finished he was taken to see the dead Hebu's body lying in the hammock, and was satisfied she had told him the truth.
summary.zh: 婦留守待行，一男子迫之曰：『不從則殺汝。』實鬼也。至其家，肉乾魚乾人肉皆懸；婦謀脫身之計：鬼喚其入吊床，辭以毛多，求竹刀為之剃面；托其頦，刺喉而殺之。攜子奔告其夫；宴罷同往視，見鬼屍在吊床，夫乃信之。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: When going to a party it is customary for the man to start early in the morning, leaving his wife to follow in the course of the afternoon. After the house-master had left for the drink-feast, another man came and paid the spouse a visit, telling her she must come with him to his place. 'No! You are not my husband, so I cannot do that.' But when he threatened to kill her if she refused, she agreed to accompany him, although her little child told her not to go. This man was really a Hebu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117A; not verbatim.

passages.text: At his house he told her she could have whatever she wanted, pointing at the dried meat — game, fish, bird, and human flesh — hanging around. All the time she was thinking how she could fool the Hebu. When he called her to come into his hammock she joined him but refused to lie down, and when he told her to kiss and coddle him she said she couldn't because he was covered over so much with hair. He told her where to find a bamboo-knife, and she commenced shaving his face; while holding up his chin, she stuck the knife into his throat and killed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117A; not verbatim.

passages.text: Rushing off with her child, the woman joined her husband at the drink-party and told him exactly what had happened: how the Hebu had made her come to his house, where she had killed him. When the sport was finished next morning she took her husband to the scene of the tragedy; as soon as he saw the dead Hebu's body lying in the hammock, he was satisfied that she had told him the truth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §117A; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bush Spirit Tricked While Hunting Frogs

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §120

summary.en: A girl who refused to go to the drink-party was visited at nightfall by a 'friend' — really a Yawahu wearing Dai-adalla's shape. Frogs croaking, they agreed to catch some in the darkness; each went her own way, calling out. 'Plenty, but I am eating them as fast as I can gather them' — the raw-eating frightened the girl, who knew then what her companion was. Hushed into silence, she slipped home, turned all the pots upside down, threw the frogs away, and climbed to the roof. The spirit groped among the many pots till dawn, groaning that he would have eaten her with the frogs, and had to leave. 'Next time we tell you to come with us, you will obey,' said the father.
summary.zh: 女不赴宴而獨守；夜有『女友』來——實鬼也。蛙鳴，相約捕捉，各往一方，呼聲相聞。『甚多，隨捉隨食』——生食也，女始知其為鬼。默然潛歸，倒置諸釜，棄蛙登屋。鬼摸索諸釜至曉而罷，恨曰：『早知汝逃，當與蛙同食汝。』父曰：『下次喚汝同行，汝必從命。』

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A family received an invitation to go to a drink-party, and all accepted except the daughter, who in spite of her parents' wishes refused to go, and was left at home alone. Late in the afternoon there came to see her a young woman friend — at least she thought it was her old friend Dai-adalla ('My-Knife'), but in reality her visitor was a Yawahu who had taken on the real friend's shape and appearance, the better to carry out his evil designs. The supposed friend offered to stay the night and keep her company.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §120; not verbatim.

passages.text: When darkness was coming on, a lot of frogs were heard croaking, and the two agreed to go straightway and catch some. Each went in an opposite direction, calling out to the other what she had caught. 'Plenty, but I am eating them as fast as I can gather them,' answered the Yawahu — a peculiar reply that frightened the girl, who thereupon recognized the real nature of her fictitious friend. When called on in turn, she shouted back: 'Hush! Don't make such noise. The frogs are getting frightened, and I shall not be able to catch any more!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §120; not verbatim.

passages.text: When silence reigned she stealthily retraced her steps, turned all the pots upside down, threw the frogs away, and climbed up on the roof to await developments. The Yawahu, receiving no response to his call, hurried back and groped about in the darkness, turning up pot after pot, but his prey was nowhere underneath. 'Ah! I would have eaten her at the same time as the frogs if I had thought she was going to get away from me,' he exclaimed, and searched until dawn. The girl descended and told her people how the Yawahu had visited her in the disguise of her friend. The father said: 'Next time we tell you to come with us, you will obey.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §120; not verbatim.

title.en: Mawari and the Tobacco Smoke

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §123

summary.en: An Indian inordinately fond of smoking puffed his way through the forest one day until Mawari, one of the Yurokons or Bush Spirits, smelled the tobacco and sent his pretty daughter to fetch the man in. Mawari begged to be taught the art, then insisted his new son-in-law remain and prepare the leaves as required. On the alligator stool the man felt a bit scared, but his wife said the creature would not bite. He stayed so long that hair began to cover his face, body, and limbs; his daughter bore him three children. Visiting his mother once, he was greeted with 'You have turned into a Yurokon, I think' — and hurried back to the bush, never returning again, forever busy preparing the tobacco for his father-in-law.
summary.zh: 一人嗜菸，終日吞雲吐霧於林中；林鬼馬瓦里聞其香，遣其美婢召之。鬼求教吸法，既得，強留其為婿治菸葉。坐鱷凳而懼，妻曰無妨。久居毛遍其身；女為之生三子。省母一次，母曰『汝化為林鬼矣』；遂返林中不復歸，終為岳父治菸。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There was once an Indian who was extremely fond of smoking: morning, noon, and night he would strike the stones together, make fire, and light his tobacco — even when walking out in the bush. While thus trudging through the forest one day and puffing out clouds of smoke, Mawari, one of the Yurokons or Bush Spirits, smelt the tobacco, took such a fancy to it, and sent his daughter to fetch the man in.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §123; not verbatim.

passages.text: She was a pretty woman, and approaching the Indian warned him that as the old Bush Spirit had really sent for him it would be wiser not to refuse; and perhaps because she was indeed so pretty, he did not hesitate to accompany her. Mawari asked a lot of questions about tobacco, begged to be taught how to smoke, and having learned the art next insisted upon the Indian remaining and preparing the tobacco leaves as they might be required. Given the alligator stool to sit upon, he felt a bit scared, but his wife told him not to be afraid, because the creature would not bite him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §123; not verbatim.

passages.text: He remained a long time with these Spirits — so long that a luxuriant growth of hair began to cover his face, body, and limbs, and Mawari's daughter bore him three children. One day his wife advised him to visit his mother, who was very glad to see him but remarked, 'Where have you been all this while? You have turned into a Yurokon, I think.' Her surmises were not far from the truth; her son denied all knowledge of those people and thought it prudent not to remain too long. He never returned home again to his mother, being ever busy preparing the tobacco for his father-in-law.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §123; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Who Mimicked the Bush Spirit

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §135

summary.en: A hunter warned his wife left at the benab that a Yawahu would pass whistling like a bird, and that if she imitated the sound each of her feet would be turned into a sharp piece of stone. Lonely, she 'called' the bird — and the Yawahu, angry, changed her feet into two sharp-pointed stones and her heart into stone also, making her wild toward her husband. She trampled the creek mud with her stony spikes hunting him, 'stuck' an alligator again and again in the full belief it was her husband; her brothers-in-law, refusing to believe, threatened the man, who led them to the benab and whistled the Yawahu's call when the spirit was safely out of hearing — the stone-footed wife came storming to destroy them all, and the forewarned brothers put an arrow into her.
summary.zh: 獵者誡留守之妻：鬼過必嘯，毋效其聲，否則雙足化尖石。婦孤而效之；鬼怒，化其足為尖石，心亦為石，遂欲殺夫。以石足踐溪泥，誤刺鱷以為夫。內兄不信，欲殺其夫；夫引至棚，俟鬼去遠而效其嘯——石足之妻暴至，欲盡誅之；兄早有備，一箭斃之。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A man went out hunting one day, taking his wife with him. Leaving her one morning at the benab, he warned her that a Yawahu would be passing and whistling like a bird, but that she must not imitate the sound in any way, because if she did each of her feet would immediately be turned into a sharp piece of stone. She had been by herself some time when she heard a bird whistling, and feeling somewhat lonely thought she would 'call' it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §135; not verbatim.

passages.text: No sooner had she imitated the sound than the Yawahu, which it really was, became extremely angry and changed her feet into two sharp-pointed stones; more than this, the Spirit changed her heart into stone also, thus making her wild toward her husband. When her husband joined her she tried to kill him; he recognized at a glance what had happened, ran to the creek, ducked and dived across, and rested on the opposite bank. She trampled the rushes and mud in all directions with her stony spikes, stamping her wrath: 'You brute! Wait till I catch you' — little knowing her husband was listening and smiling all the while, until at last she stuck one of her feet into an alligator lying there and 'stuck' it again and again in the full belief that it was her husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §135; not verbatim.

passages.text: His brothers-in-law would not believe what he said about her having mimicked the Yawahu, and finally tried to kill him. Seeing them threatening him, he offered to show them the actual place where it all happened. Reaching the benab — no wife was there — the husband imitated the Yawahu's whistle, now that the Spirit was nowhere in the neighborhood and well out of hearing: and who should come running up but his stone-footed wife, storming with rage, ready to destroy not only her man but her brothers also. The brothers, however, being forewarned, put an arrow into her, and she fell dead; they knew now that the man had spoken the truth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §135; not verbatim.

title.en: The Danger of Associating with Spirits

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. VIII 'Spirits of the Bush', §§136-138

summary.en: Two brothers deep in the forest heard the revelry of a drinking-party; the elder insisted on joining, though the younger warned they must be Spirits. At the house — really the Spirits of the great Rain-frogs in human shape — the elder drank and was happy. That night his feet kept drifting into the fire however much his brother piled on fuel; when he finally looked down, both feet were entirely gone, and he cleaned the flesh off and scraped his shin-bones down to sharp points. Spear-birds from his hammock with his bone points, he pursued his 'runaway' brother, pinned a deer, counted five fingers and five toes against his own three-and-three, and knew he had killed the wrong creature. Then the others surrounded his benab and decoyed him out with a squirrel to destroy him.
summary.zh: 兄弟聞林中宴樂聲；兄執意往，弟言其必鬼。至則大雨蛙之鬼幻形為人；兄暢飲。夜其足頻近火而不覺；後視之，雙足已盡失，遂剝肉削脛骨為銳尖。以骨尖自吊床刺鳥獸，追所謂『逃去』之弟，誤釘一鹿；數其指趾五五，自省僅三三，知殺錯。眾遂圍其棚，以松鼠誘之出而誅之。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: There were two brothers living together, both of whom used to go hunting. Deep in the heart of the forest they heard the sounds and revelry of a drinking-party. 'Come, let us go sport with those people,' said the elder; but the younger replied: 'No! It can not be a real party out here in the bush away from everybody: they must be Spirits of some sort.' The big brother insisted. At the house apparently real people were enjoying themselves; the visitors were made to sit down and drinks handed to them. The elder indulged and was happy; the younger refused because he was afraid — for the revelers were really not people at all but the Spirits of the Warekki, the large Rain-frogs, in human shape.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §136; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the benab that night the elder told his brother again and again to put more wood on the fire, until an immense blaze was going. Then the younger man smelt a very peculiar strong odor and saw his brother's legs hanging from the hammock close over the fire. 'Look out! your legs are getting scorched.' All his brother did was to draw his feet in, and put them into danger again — a token of some evil, for he had not even been drunk at the party. When he finally realized his lower limbs were charred, both feet were entirely gone; all he did was clean the flesh off entirely and scrape both shin-bones down to sharp points, lying helpless in his hammock, though now and again he would spear a passing bird with the pointed tips, a trick in which he soon became expert.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§136-137; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sick man kept calling his brother back before he could even shoot, until the younger, threatened with death if he left his sight, escaped under an excuse. The crippled man pursued, found with his bone points he could travel faster than on feet, pinned a deer — 'I am sorry, Brother, to have killed you, but it is your own fault' — then counted the animal's five fingers and five toes against his own three and three, and concluded it could not possibly be his brother. In the meantime the fugitive reached home: 'Something has happened to my brother. We must kill him.' They surrounded his benab, sent a swift little squirrel to decoy him onto the open — and when he got quite near, fell upon and destroyed him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§137-138; not verbatim.
